# CHAPTER XXIV

INDIAN SUMMER (1898-1899)

The summer of the Spanish War began the Indian summer of life to one who had reached sixty years of age, and cared only to reap in peace such harvest as these sixty years had yielded. Since 1864 he had felt no such sense of power and momentum, and seen no such number of personal friends wielding it. In London, in 1898, the scene was singularly interesting to the last survivor of the Legation of 1861. He carried every scene of it, in a century and a half since the Stamp Act, quite alive in his mind. After two hundred years of stupid and greedy blundering, which no argument and no violence affected, the people of England learned their lesson just at the moment when Hay would otherwise have faced a flood of the old anxieties; and suddenly, by pure chance, the blessing fell on Hay. To Adams, still living in the atmosphere of Palmerston and John Russell, the sudden appearance of Germany as the grizzly terror which, in twenty years, effected what Adamses had tried for two hundred in vain—frightened England into America's arms—seemed as melodramatic as any plot of Napoleon the Great.

This was history, not education, yet it taught something serious. For the first time in his life, he felt a sense of possible purpose working itself out in history. Sitting at Hay's table, listening to any member of the British Cabinet discuss the Philippines as a question of balance of power in the East, he could see the family work of a hundred and fifty years fall at once into the grand perspective of true empire-building, which Hay's work set off with artistic skill. Never before had Adams been able to discern the working of law in history, which was the reason of his failure in teaching it, for chaos cannot be taught. Education on the outskirts of civilized life teaches not very much, but it taught this; and after all, friends had done the work, if not one's self, and he too serves a certain purpose who only stands and cheers.

In June, the Camerons came over and took the fine old house of Surrenden Dering in Kent, which they made a sort of country house to the Embassy. There, on a hot July 4, 1898, came the telegram announcing the destruction of the Spanish Armada, as it might have come to Queen Elizabeth in 1588; and there, later, came the order summoning Hay to the State Department.

Hay had no wish to be Secretary of State. He much preferred to remain Ambassador, and his friends were quite as cold about it as he. The decided voice of the conclave was that, though if he were a mere office-seeker he might decline promotion, if he were a member of the Government he could not. No serious statesman could accept a favor and refuse a service. For Adams, no one in his experience had ever passed unscathed through that malarious marsh. Office was poison; it killed—body and soul—physically and socially. The poison was that of the will—the distortion of sight—the warping of mind—the degradation of tissue—the coarsening of taste—the narrowing of sympathy to the emotions of a caged rat. Hay needed no office in order to wield influence; influence lay about the streets, waiting for him to stoop to it. At sixty years of age, he took office at cost of life.

He shouldered his pack and started for home; on November 13, none too gladly, Adams found himself again gazing into La Fayette Square. He had nothing to do with Hay's politics at home or abroad, and never affected agreement with his views or his methods. They all united in trying to help each other along, and all they tried to save was the personal relation. Adams would have been beaten had he not been helped by Mrs. Hay, who saw the necessity of distraction, and led her husband into the habit of stopping every afternoon to take his friend off for an hour's walk, followed by a cup of tea afterwards.

On March 22, Adams sailed with the Lodges for Europe, and passed April in Sicily and Rome. With the Lodges, education always began afresh. Forty years had left little of the Palermo that Garibaldi had shown to the boy of 1860, but Sicily in all ages seems to have taught only catastrophe and violence. For a lesson in anarchy, without a shade of sequence, Sicily stands alone and defies evolution. Yet even Rome was not mute, and the church of Ara Cœli seemed more and more to draw all the threads of thought to a centre, for every new journey led back to its steps—Karnak, Ephesus, Delphi, Mycenæ, Constantinople, Syracuse—all lying on the road to the Capitol. In forty years, America had made so vast a stride to empire that the world of 1860 stood already on a distant horizon somewhere on the same plane with the republic of Brutus and Cato. The climax of empire could be seen approaching, year after year, as though Sulla were a President or McKinley a Consul.

By way of completing the lesson, the Lodges added a pilgrimage to Assisi and an interview with St. Francis, whose solution of historical riddles seemed the most satisfactory ever offered. The most bewildering effect of all these fresh cross-lights on the old Assistant Professor of 1874 was due to the astonishing contrast between what he had taught then and what he found himself confusedly trying to learn five-and-twenty years afterwards. At Harvard College, weary of spirit in the wastes of Anglo-Saxon law, he had occasionally given way to outbursts of derision at shedding his life-blood for the sublime truths of Sac and Soc:—

HIC JACET
HOMUNCULUS SCRIPTOR
DOCTOR BARBARICUS
HENRICUS ADAMS
ADAE FILIUS ET EVAE
PRIMO EXPLICUIT
SOCNAM

The whole point of view had vanished in 1900. The law had proved as futile as politics or religion, or any other single thread spun by the human spider. St. Francis expressed supreme contempt for them all, and solved the whole problem by rejecting it altogether. Adams returned to Paris with a broken and contrite spirit, prepared to admit that his life had no meaning. He passed a summer of solitude that forced him into the study of his ignorance in silence, and began a methodical survey—a triangulation—of the twelfth century. In the long summer days one found a sort of saturated green pleasure in the forests, and gray infinity of rest in the little twelfth-century churches that lined them, as unassuming as their own mosses, and as sure of their purpose as their round arches.

His solitude was broken in November by the chance arrival of John La Farge. Of all his friends, La Farge alone owned a mind complex enough to contrast against the commonplaces of American uniformity. The American mind likes to walk straight up to its object, and assert or deny something that it takes for a fact. The most disconcerting trait of La Farge was his reversal of the process. His approach was quiet and indirect; he moved round an object, and never separated it from its surroundings. As he said of his friend Okakura, his thought ran as a stream runs through grass, hidden perhaps but always there. "Adams, you reason too much!" was one of his standing reproaches. He should have blamed Adams for being born in Boston. To La Farge, eccentricity meant convention; a mind really eccentric never betrayed it. True eccentricity was a tone—a shade—a nuance. Whatever else he brought, La Farge led Adams back to the twelfth century and to Chartres, where La Farge alone could use glass like a thirteenth-century artist.

Adams got him safely back to New York, January 15, 1900, and went at once to Washington. Hay's troubles had begun, and were quite as great as he had foreseen. But all this worry on Hay's account fretted him not nearly so much as the Boer War did on his own. To Adams the war became almost a personal outrage. He had been taught from childhood, even in England, that his forbears and their associates in 1776 had settled, once for all, the liberties of the British free colonies, and he very strongly objected to being thrown on the defensive again, and forced to sit down, a hundred and fifty years after John Adams had begun the task, to prove, by appeal to law and fact, that George Washington was not a felon, whatever might be the case with George III.

With Hay's politics Adams had nothing whatever to do. Hay belonged to the New York school—men who played the game for ambition or amusement, and played it, as a rule, much better than the professionals. President McKinley undertook to pool interests in a general trust into which every interest should be taken at its own valuation, and whose mass should, under his management, create efficiency. But abroad, whatever helped on one side hurt him on another. Hay thought England must be brought first into the combine; but at that time Germany, Russia, and France were all combining against England, and the Boer War helped them. Yet the difficulty abroad was far less troublesome than the obstacles at home, where the Senate had grown more and more unmanageable.

"A treaty of peace, in any normal state of things," said Hay, "ought to be ratified with unanimity in twenty-four hours. They wasted six weeks in wrangling over this one, and ratified it with one vote to spare. We have five or six matters now demanding settlement. I can settle them all, honorably and advantageously to our own side; and I am assured by leading men in the Senate that not one of these treaties, if negotiated, will pass the Senate. I should have a majority in every case, but a malcontent third would certainly dish every one of them. To such monstrous shape has the original mistake of the Constitution grown in the evolution of our politics. Is it worth while—for me—to keep up this useless labor?"

The fathers had intended to neutralize the energy of government and had succeeded, but their machine was never meant to do the work of a twenty-million horse-power society in the twentieth century. Always unselfish, generous, easy, patient, and loyal, Hay had treated the world as something to be taken in block without pulling it to pieces to get rid of its defects. Yet even the gayest of tempers succumbs at last to constant friction. The old friend was rapidly fading. The habit remained, but the easy intimacy, the careless gaiety, the casual humor, the equality of indifference, were sinking into the routine of office.

Although this branch of study was older than the twelfth century, the task of bringing the two periods into a common relation was new. Ignorance required that these political and social and scientific values of the twelfth and twentieth centuries should be correlated in some relation of movement that could be expressed in mathematics, nor did one care that all the world said it could not be done, or that one knew not enough mathematics even to figure a formula beyond the schoolboy s = gt²/2. If Kepler and Newton could take liberties with the sun and moon, an obscure person in La Fayette Square could take liberties with Congress.

All his associates in history condemned such an attempt as futile and almost immoral. He had pursued ignorance thus far with success, and had swept his mind clear of knowledge. In beginning again, from the starting-point of Sir Isaac Newton, he looked about him in vain for a teacher. The most accessible was Langley, of the Smithsonian, to whom Adams had been much in the habit of turning whenever he wanted an outlet for his vast reservoirs of ignorance. Langley listened with outward patience, but he too nourished a scientific passion for doubt. Like most physicists, he believed in physics. He early put into Adams's hands the "Concepts of Modern Science," a volume by Judge Stallo, which had been treated for a dozen years by the schools with a conspiracy of silence such as inevitably meets every revolutionary work that upsets the stock and machinery of instruction. Adams read and failed to understand; then he asked questions and failed to get answers.

Probably this was education. For him the details of science meant nothing: he wanted to know its mass. History had no use for multiplicity; it needed unity; it could study only motion, direction, attraction, relation. Everything must be made to move together; one must seek new worlds to measure; and so, like Rasselas, Adams set out once more, and found himself on May 12 settled in rooms at the very door of the Trocadero.
